sections.h2: Who bills, collects and values in Troy
sections.html:
Troy's summer and winter bills come from the City Treasurer's Office in City Hall at 500 W Big Beaver Road, which keeps weekday hours of 8 to 4:30. Troy lies in Oakland County, and the county treasurer picks up whatever the city has not collected by March 1.

One Troy bill funds many bodies. Besides city services, the city collects and passes along tax for seven school districts, the county, the Huron-Clinton Metropolitan Authority, the county's art, zoo and transit authorities, Oakland Schools and the Macomb Intermediate School District. A house's school district shapes the millage, which is why the city posts a Millage Rates page.

The City Assessor's Office covers values. It appraises each parcel, processes splits and combinations, and runs the Principal Residence Exemption and Property Transfer Affidavit programs. Call it at 248-524-3311.

Summer statements are mailed July 1 and winter statements December 1. A deadline that falls on a weekend or city holiday slides forward one business day, as with the 2026 winter bills, which run through February 16, 2027.

Troy payment deadlines and penalties
BillMailedPay byPenalty after the deadline
SummerJuly 1September 14% the first business day after, then one-half of 1% monthly interest from October 1
WinterDecember 1February 143% the first business day after
Any unpaid current-year billNot applicableMarch 1Sent to Oakland County as delinquent, with fees and interest on top

A bill that never arrived is no excuse, and penalty and interest still apply. After March 1, payment goes to the Oakland County Treasurer in Pontiac at 248.858.0611, option 7. Ask for the current amount owing, because fees keep building.

Troy accepts automatic debit, mail, cards, e-checks, bank bill pay and walk-in payment. A check or money order placed in an official drop box before 8 a.m. on the business day following a due date still counts as on time.

  • Automatic debit from checking or savings costs nothing, and for winter you choose February 14 or the last business day of December.
  • Cards cost 3%, with a floor of $1.50 online and $2.00 at the counter. E-checks are free below $10,000 and $10 from $10,000 up.
  • Red and blue Official Drop Boxes stand outside City Hall's east walk-up and west drive-up doors, for checks and money orders only.
  • Walk in with the entire statement. Cash, checks, money orders and cards are all taken.

The city's BS&A lookup prints bills and shows payments once you register, which costs nothing. A cleared check is the best receipt, and the city will mail a paper one if you send a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

sections.h2: Help for owners who cannot pay on time
sections.html:
Qualifying households can defer. A Property Tax Deferment moves the due date on both bills to the following April 30. Household income has to be $40,000 or less, and the owner must be 62 or older, paraplegic, hemiplegic or quadriplegic, totally and permanently disabled or blind, or an eligible service person, veteran, widow or widower.

Apply on Michigan Treasury Form 471, delivered to the Treasurer's Office by September 15 with last year's Homestead Property Tax Credit form attached. Questions go to 248.524.3333. Owners outside those groups avoid the March 1 transfer only by paying the winter bill in full on time.

Troy's 2026 roll holds 35,732 parcels with assessed value of $10,026,428,690 and taxable value of $7,270,919,530. Those totals are up 5.76% and 4.47% on 2025.

Residential real property makes up 28,149 parcels, with assessed value of $6,866,814,460. The average residential parcel carries an assessed value of $243,945, an estimated average market value of $487,890 and an average taxable value of $174,224. In 2025 the city logged 759 valid single-family sales averaging $530,076, with a low of $120,000 and a high of $1,850,000, plus 245 condominium sales averaging $375,029.

The gap between assessed and taxable value matters when you sell. Assessed value follows the market, while taxable value is capped for as long as one owner holds the home. The next owner's first bill is usually higher than yours.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Troy assessment?
sections.html:
For a Troy homeowner, the March Board of Review is the single chance to contest a residential value, and a missed session means waiting a year. Mid-February brings a notice of assessment to every property whose assessed value changed, listing protest dates. If it never reaches you, the values still stand.

When city appraisers visit, they carry marked badges and measure the outside of the house and any improvements. Participation is voluntary, and staff do not need to enter the home, although they ask about the interior and mail a survey. General maintenance such as new gutters, a roof or windows is not assessable. What raises value is air conditioning, decks, porches, patios, sheds, additions, garages, finished basements and added bathrooms. Appointments run through the Assessing Department, with field slots between 9:00 a.m. and 2:30 p.m.

The department processed about 2,448 recorded deeds in 2025, and most produced a Property Transfer Affidavit. It handles a similar number of Principal Residence Exemption affidavits each year. Businesses must file personal property statements by February 20.

Troy covers about 33.5 square miles and sits on Interstate 75. Somerset Collection and Oakland Mall anchor retail, and Amtrak's Wolverine train stops at the Troy Transit Center. Seven districts reach into Troy. Troy School District serves most addresses, with Troy High School and Athens High School as its two zoned high schools. Avondale, Birmingham and Warren Consolidated also run schools inside the city, so confirm the district for any address you are marketing.

The city has 88,733 residents. Nearly three of four homes (73.3%) are owner-occupied, at a median value of $420,300, and median household income is $120,045. Recent sales on your own street will say more than any citywide median.

Before you list, ask the Treasurer for the balance on each bill and let the title company settle it from proceeds. The buyer files the Property Transfer Affidavit with Assessing, and a seller who claimed the Principal Residence Exemption should ask Assessing how to end it. Cash buyers skip the lender's escrow step, which makes the payoff figure the main item to line up.

faqs.q: What is the penalty if I pay my Troy summer bill late?
faqs.a: A 4% penalty is added on the first business day after September 1, and one-half of 1% monthly interest starts October 1. The winter bill carries a 3% penalty after February 14.

faqs.q: When does my Troy tax bill go to Oakland County?
faqs.a: On March 1, every unpaid current-year bill is transferred to the Oakland County Treasurer as delinquent, with added fees and interest. Pay the county at 1200 N Telegraph Rd, Dept 479, Pontiac, or call 248.858.0611, option 7.

faqs.q: Can I have a Troy payment taken from my bank automatically?
faqs.a: Yes, at no fee. Troy withdraws the payment on the due date, and a separate enrollment form is needed for property tax and for water and sewer. For the winter bill you choose February 14 or the last business day in December.

faqs.q: Who do I call in Troy about my home's value?
faqs.a: Call the Assessing Department at 248-524-3311. Office hours are Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and appraiser visits can be booked for slots between 9:00 a.m. and 2:30 p.m.

faqs.q: How much time do Troy owners have to appeal a residential value?
faqs.a: The only window is the March Board of Review, and it applies to the current year. If you miss it, you give up the right to appeal that year's value.
